item.title: Deadly Airborne Spores Infect Pets in 31 Areas
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection that is most often seen in outdoor dogs and cats, and hunting dogs
  • There can be a wide range of symptoms from the infection, depending on which organs of your pet’s body are affected
  • In mild cases of respiratory histoplasmosis, often the pet is able to clear the infection without medical intervention
  • More severe infections may require hospitalization initially, and a long course of antifungal therapy
  • Functional medicine and integrative veterinarians also use adjunctive therapies to help histoplasmosis patients recover more quickly and comfortably

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 26, 2018.

Histoplasmosis is an infection caused by the Histoplasma capsulatum fungus, which is found in soil, most commonly in warm, moist, humid conditions. In the U.S., the fungus has been reported in 31 states, primarily in the midwest and south, especially along the Mississippi, Missouri and Ohio rivers. Areas with bird and/or bat droppings are also friendly environments for the fungus.

Histoplasma fungi produce tiny airborne spores that are heat-resistant and can be inhaled by pets. The spores engage the immune system, reproduce in immune system cells and then travel throughout the body in the bloodstream. They ultimately wind up in the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, lymph nodes, bone marrow, lungs, liver and spleen.

Both dogs and cats can acquire histoplasmosis, but the infection is most often seen in outside dogs and cats and particularly hunting dogs. A few cases of infection in strictly indoor animals have been reported, but it’s rare and it is suspected that potting soil or dirt brought in from outside is the source of infection in these animals. Pets of any age can be affected, but most infections occur in animals under the age of four.

Symptoms of Histoplasmosis

Symptoms of infection range from none to severe. The nature and extent of symptoms depends on the organ systems infected by the fungi. Histoplasmosis may be confined to just the lungs or just the GI tract, or it can become systemic, infecting the whole body. Symptoms include:

  • Loss of appetite
  • Bloody stool
  • Depression
  • Vomiting
  • Weight loss
  • Mucous or fat in the stool
  • Difficult or labored breathing
  • Muscle wasting
  • Diarrhea
  • Exercise intolerance
  • Cough (usually chronic)
  • Enlarged tonsils
  • Straining to defecate
  • Lethargy
  • Fever
  • Enlarged lymph nodes

As the infection progresses, pets can become emaciated, have elevated heart and respiration rates, lameness, and ulcerated sores on the skin or around the eyes. In addition to the GI and respiratory tracts, histoplasmosis can affect a number of other organ systems including the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bones and bone marrow, adrenal glands, kidneys, testes, and the mouth, tongue and eyes.

Diagnosing Histoplasmosis

Your veterinarian will take a history of your pet’s overall health and symptoms and perform a thorough physical examination. He or she will note important changes such as abnormal lung sounds, pale mucous membranes, changes in your pet’s heart or respiratory rate, an enlarged liver or spleen, lymph node enlargement, lameness or joint swelling, and any eye abnormalities.

A complete blood count (CBC) will be ordered, along with a serum biochemical profile to check internal organ function, and a urinalysis. However, while blood tests can confirm the presence of histoplasmosis antibodies, this only means your pet has been exposed to the fungus, and not necessarily that she’s developed disease as the result of exposure.

The presence of antibodies will prompt further differential testing to confirm an infection, and can include urine screening for the fungus, chest X-rays, aspiration of the liver and spleen, taking lung fluid samples, bone X-rays or biopsies, GI biopsies, and a spinal tap. Since the symptoms of histoplasmosis are also present with a number of other diseases, it’s critically important that a confirming diagnosis of histoplasmosis is made.

Treatment Options

In mild cases of the respiratory form of histoplasmosis, treatment may not be necessary, because your pet’s body may mount an effective immune response and clear the infection on its own. If the infection is severe, aggressive treatment with antifungal medication may be needed to save your pet’s life. Medications used to treat histoplasmosis include itraconazole, fluconazole, ketoconazole and amphotericin B.

In mild cases, antifungals are given orally for four to six months. That may seem like a long time, but whereas antibiotics can resolve bacterial infections quite quickly in most cases, antifungal therapy takes considerably longer. Typically, veterinarians prescribe antifungal drugs for a minimum of four months.

In severe cases of histoplasmosis requiring hospitalization, intravenous (IV) antifungal medications may also be given, along with oxygen, IV fluids and nutritional support as necessary.

Unfortunately, like all drugs, antifungals have a number of potential adverse side effects, especially involving the GI tract. They are also expensive, especially for large and giant breed dogs. Amphotericin B also carries a high risk for kidney damage, so most people opt to use some of the safer antifungal drugs.

Your integrative veterinarian will probably suggest adjunctive therapies, like nebulization therapy if the fungus is in the lungs, or ozone therapy if there is a systemic infection. Many animals also benefit from IV vitamin C therapy, which provides tremendous antioxidant and immune system support.

As with any illness, the sooner your pet is diagnosed and treated for histoplasmosis, the better. The prognosis is good if the correct treatment is given before the animal becomes debilitated.

item.title: Could Your Pet's Heart Be Asking for Help?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Heart disease is common in middle-aged and senior dogs, but early stages usually have no obvious symptoms
  • The warning signs worth knowing include a new cough (especially at night), faster breathing at rest, tiring more easily, fainting or collapse, restlessness at night, and a swollen belly. At the same time, labored breathing, collapse, or pale, gray, or bluish gums are same-day emergencies
  • The single most useful home monitoring habit is counting your dog's resting or sleeping breathing rate: a consistently rising rate, or one above 30 breaths per minute, is often the earliest sign that fluid may be backing up in the lungs
  • The most common conditions are mitral valve disease (MMVD) in small breeds and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in large breeds
  • With early diagnosis, tailored medications, a heart-friendly lower-sodium diet, weight management, gentle exercise, and consistent monitoring, many dogs with heart disease enjoy a good quality of life for months to years after diagnosis

Your dog seems a little quieter than usual. They still greet you at the door, still finish their food, still curl up on the couch. But they slow down halfway through a walk that used to be no problem. There's a soft cough after they lie down. Their breathing looks a bit faster than you remember, even while they sleep.

These small changes are easy to dismiss as a natural part of aging. Sometimes they are. Other times, they are subtle signs your pet's heart needs help. Recognizing the signs early is one of the biggest gifts you can offer them.

Why Hearts Are So Good at Hiding Trouble

Heart disease is common in dogs, especially in middle age and beyond. But the earliest stages usually have no obvious symptoms at all. Many pets look and act completely normal even as their heart is already changing.

The first hint is often something a veterinarian picks up during a routine physical exam: a heart murmur or an irregular rhythm heard through a stethoscope. That may be the only signal for months or even years before other symptoms surface.

It's part of why yearly wellness visits are important and why twice-yearly exams are recommended for older pets. By the time visible signs appear, the underlying condition may have been progressing quietly for a while.1,2,3

Warning Signs Worth Knowing

Even though early heart disease is often silent, there are specific changes that should prompt a call to your vet. Take your pet to the clinic if you notice these signs:4,5,6

  • A new or worsening cough, especially at night or after lying down
  • Faster or harder breathing at rest or while sleeping
  • Tiring easily or falling behind on walks that used to be routine
  • Reluctance to play or exercise
  • Fainting, collapse, or sudden weakness
  • A visibly swollen or bloated belly
  • Restlessness at night or trouble getting comfortable
  • A mild drop in appetite
  • Weight loss

Some signs are outright emergencies. Labored breathing, collapse, extreme lethargy, or gums that look pale, gray, or bluish need same-day emergency care, so don’t wait.

The Home Tool Every Heart Pet Parent Should Know

One of the most useful, low-tech monitoring habits in veterinary cardiology is the resting or sleeping respiratory rate. It costs nothing, takes 60 seconds, and can give you an early warning that something has changed.7

When your dog is truly asleep or resting calmly (not panting or dreaming), count the rise and fall of their chest for 30 seconds and double it. A healthy dog usually breathes fewer than 30 breaths per minute at rest.8,9

A consistently higher rate, or a rate that keeps trending upward over days or weeks, is a red flag that fluid may be building up in the lungs. Track it a few times a week if your dog has a known heart condition, and share the numbers with your vet. It is one of the earliest, most reliable clues you can catch at home.

The Main Heart Conditions in Dogs

Several different heart conditions can affect dogs. The terminology can get confusing, so here are the ones that come up most often:10,11,12

  • Heart murmur — Murmurs come from turbulent blood flow, often caused by a valve that isn't closing properly. A murmur is not a disease itself, but a sound, and can be a very early clue that something needs attention.
  • Mitral valve disease — Also called myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), this is the most common acquired heart disease in dogs. The mitral valve, which controls blood flow on the left side of the heart, gradually thickens and leaks. Blood flows backward within the heart instead of moving forward efficiently.
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) — This is a disease of the heart muscle itself rather than the valves. The heart muscle weakens and stretches, the chambers enlarge, and pumping ability drops.
  • Congestive heart failure (CHF) — It’s not a disease on its own but a syndrome. It develops when a diseased heart can no longer keep up with the body's demands, and fluid backs up into the lungs or abdomen. Both MMVD and DCM can eventually lead to CHF.

The Valves, Explained Simply

Think of the heart's four valves as one-way doors. Each one opens to let blood through and closes to keep it from flowing backward. When a valve gets thick, leaky, or damaged, the door stops sealing properly. Three valve conditions in particular come up in dogs:13

  • Mitral valve disease is by far the most common. The mitral valve sits between the upper and lower chambers on the left side of the heart. When it degenerates, blood leaks backward. Small breeds and Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, in particular, have a well-known genetic risk.
  • Tricuspid valve insufficiency involves the valve on the right side of the heart. Leaks here can cause fluid to build up in the abdomen and lead to serious complications if unmanaged.
  • Aortic insufficiency happens when the aortic valve, which controls the flow of blood out of the heart to the rest of the body, does not close properly. This one is sometimes linked to bacterial infections of the heart, a condition called endocarditis.

Which Pets Are Most at Risk

Some pets are more likely to develop heart disease than others. The biggest risk factors are:14,15

  • Breed — Small breeds like Cavalier King Charles Spaniels, Chihuahuas, Dachshunds, and toy breeds are at highest risk for mitral valve disease. Large and giant breeds like Doberman Pinschers, Great Danes, Boxers, and Irish Wolfhounds are at higher risk for DCM.
  • Age — Risk rises significantly with age, especially past middle age.
  • Size — Dogs under 40 pounds (lbs.) have a higher risk of MMVD; dogs over 60 lbs. are more prone to DCM.
  • Body condition — Excess weight puts additional strain on the cardiovascular system.
  • Family history (when it's known).

Cats can also develop heart disease, though the most common feline condition is a different one (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Many of the same warning signs, such as increased breathing at rest, lethargy, and poor appetite, apply.

A Word About Diet and DCM

In recent years, there has been increasing attention on a possible link between certain diets and dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs who are not from typical DCM breeds. Diets marketed as grain-free or boutique, or those high in legumes such as peas and lentils, have been investigated as possible contributors.

Research is still evolving, and no one food ingredient has been definitively identified as the cause. But if your dog eats a grain-free or non-traditional diet, it is worth talking with your vet about whether a change might be reasonable, especially if your dog is in a higher-risk group.16

How Vets Diagnose Heart Disease

The workup usually starts with the basics: a full physical exam, questions about your pet's energy, appetite, sleep, and any changes at home, and a careful listen to the heart and lungs. If your vet finds a murmur, an irregular rhythm, or fluid in the lungs, they may recommend:17,18,19

  • Chest X-rays to assess heart size and look for fluid in the lungs
  • An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart), considered the gold standard for visualizing structure and function
  • An electrocardiogram (ECG) to evaluate heart rhythm
  • Blood pressure measurement
  • Cardiac biomarker blood tests like NT-proBNP, which can indicate stress on the heart

For a precise diagnosis and staging, a board-certified veterinary cardiologist may be brought in. Early, accurate staging matters because it directly shapes the treatment plan.

How Heart Disease Is Managed

Treatment depends on the type, stage, and severity of the condition, and your vet always guides it. In general, management may include:20,21,22

  • Medications — Depending on the diagnosis, your vet may prescribe drugs that help the heart pump more efficiently (like pimobendan), diuretics to reduce fluid buildup, medications to control blood pressure, or drugs to manage abnormal rhythms.
  • Prescription cardiac diets — These are typically lower in sodium and formulated to support cardiovascular function. Your vet may recommend one based on your dog's specific stage of disease.
  • Weight management — Excess weight makes the heart work harder. Getting to a healthy body condition is one of the most impactful things you can do for a pet with heart disease.
  • Sensible exercise — Gentle, consistent activity like short calm walks supports circulation and overall cardiovascular fitness. Intense activity should be scaled back as disease progresses, always following your vet's guidance.
  • Regular monitoring — Repeat imaging, biomarker testing, and at-home tracking of resting breathing rate help your vet adjust the plan as your pet's needs change.

The good news is, with early diagnosis, consistent care, and regular follow-up, many dogs with heart disease enjoy a good quality of life for months to years after diagnosis.

Supportive Nutrition and Lifestyle

Beyond prescription treatments, several supportive strategies can help keep the cardiovascular system in the best shape possible. Always discuss these with your vet before making changes, especially if your pet is already on a specific diet or medication.

Certain nutrients have supporting roles in normal heart function. Taurine, L-carnitine, coenzyme Q10, L-arginine, and omega-3 fatty acids each play a part in cardiovascular biology. Omega-3s from fish oil, in particular, have anti-inflammatory benefits that may support heart health.

Antioxidant-rich whole foods like blueberries, leafy greens, and sweet potatoes may also support overall health. Any additions to the diet should be coordinated with your vet, especially if your pet is on a prescription cardiac diet.

Chronic stress does not do the heart any favors either. A calm home environment, a predictable routine, and quiet retreat spaces all support the nervous system, which in turn supports the cardiovascular system. Some pet parents use gentle massage or acupuncture as complementary approaches under veterinary guidance.23,24,25

Living with a Pet Who Has Heart Disease

A heart diagnosis is scary. It changes how you look at your pet, at their food bowl, at their morning walk. But it does not have to be a death sentence, and it does not have to mean the immediate end of the life you have been enjoying together.

With the right team, your primary vet, a cardiologist when needed, and a personalized plan, you can extend both the length and the quality of your pet's life. Many owners describe their dog acting like themselves again once early treatment kicks in: more energy, less coughing, a better appetite, easier breathing.

Staying on top of medications, keeping regular follow-up appointments, tracking that resting breathing rate at home, and being alert for changes are the everyday habits that make the biggest difference over time.

Listen for the Quiet Signals

Hearts are patient. They keep beating through a lot, they compensate for a lot, and they are astonishingly good at hiding trouble until they can't anymore. That is exactly why the quiet signals — a slower walk, a soft cough, breathing that seems a little faster than usual — are so important.

If you notice any of the warning signs, book a visit with your vet. If you have an older pet or one from a higher-risk breed, ask about heart-focused screening even if nothing seems wrong. And if your pet has already been diagnosed with a heart condition, know that a good plan and a watchful eye at home can add real time and real quality to the years you have together.

Your pet's heart has been doing quiet work for you their entire life. Answering when it finally asks for help is one of the most loving things you can offer back.

Sources and References

  • 1,4,10,14,16,17,20,23 Chewy, June 26, 2026
  • 2,5,9,11,13,15,18,21,24 Animal Wellness Magazine, June 26, 2026
  • 3,6,7,8,12,19,22,25 Dr. Fossum’s Pet Care, June 2026

item.title: Hazards to Avoid While Baking Homemade Dog Treats
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • If your dog is on a special diet to prevent urinary stone formation, food allergies or sensitivities, treat ingredients can counteract that diet
  • Toxic ingredients, including a common sweetener called xylitol, are important to avoid when making dog treats
  • Talk to your veterinarian for insight regarding your dog’s needs, especially because baking treats in your own kitchen for your dog to enjoy won’t have much of an impact nutritionally if your dog’s optimal health suffers as a consequence
  • Treats shouldn’t comprise more than 10% of the calorie intake your dog consumes on a daily basis, with the remaining 90% derived from a complete and balanced fresh species-appropriate diet
  • When it comes to baking dog treats you know your dog will love, take care to give them something that will enhance their health, not detract from it

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 22, 2019.

Making treats for your dog rather than purchasing the kinds manufactured by most companies that specialize in them is a wise decision, as the majority of them are loaded with sugar, preservatives, flavorings and colorings that aren’t just unnatural. They can be very unhealthy for your dog’s digestive system, not to mention other bodily systems as well.

Unfortunately, you can’t always trust labels that assure dog treats are “all natural.” So what’s the best way to give your canine companion a little something extra, but ensure it’s something that will be nutritious as well as enjoyable? Making your own dog treats, which will help address special dietary needs your dog may have and avoid potential dietary problems, such as obesity.1

Although it may seem a bit intimidating, with a few basic guidelines it shouldn’t break the bank or contribute to poor health. Susan Jeffrey, a veterinarian at Truesdell Animal Care Hospital in Madison, Wisconsin, says that if your dog is on a special diet to prevent urinary stone formation or something similar, treat ingredients can counteract that diet, and the same can be said for dogs with food allergies and sensitivities.

Needless to say, sugar- and frosting-coated treats are completely unnecessary, unhealthy and probably not even something dogs enjoy that much. Also, Jeffrey asserts, avoiding fat is important because some dogs can develop pancreatitis with high-fat treats and foods, especially if it’s hydrogenated or “interesterified.” Pancreatitis is a painful inflammation of the pancreas that can result in hospitalization for a pet.

As always, talk to your veterinarian for insight regarding your dog’s needs, especially because baking treats in your own kitchen for your dog to enjoy won’t have much of an impact nutritionally if your dog’s optimal health suffers as a consequence. So what are good ingredients to put in your dog’s treats? PetMD notes:

“Many vegetables and fruits are a safe bet … include[ing] broccoli, carrots, summer squash, zucchini, Brussels sprouts, pumpkin, cucumber, celery, spinach, kale, dandelion greens, apple (and unsweetened apple sauce), peaches, pears, strawberries, blueberries and bananas.”2

Often, certain human foods such as fresh meats, berries and raw almonds in homemade dog treats are far better for your dog compared to most commercially processed treats. It’s important to look for organic produce whenever possible, to avoid excessive pesticide ingestion. And one of the biggest problems comes with dog bones given as treats, because they’re also known as recreational, but they’re not for all dogs.

It’s important to note that raw bones are the safest, but all chews can have consequences so always supervise your dog while he's working on a bone — don't let him out of your sight.

Things to Watch for When Preparing Dog Treats

That said, not everything that’s good for humans is beneficial for dogs, and some ingredients can be toxic enough to cause serious illnesses, even to the point of fatality. Here are a few other points to consider when embarking on your dog treat-making venture.

  • One ingredient to watch for is xylitol, which is relatively new in the sweetener lineup. It’s often used to (in the minds of some) make mints and chewable vitamins, as well as baked goods and some prescription medications, more palatable. While the granulated form of xylitol, a sugar alcohol, is one of the better alternative sweeteners for protein bars, coffee, tea and other beverages intended for humans, it’s not for dogs.

    In fact, it’s extremely harmful for dogs, and it only takes a little to be dangerous. Symptoms of xylitol ingestion include vomiting, seizures, difficulty walking, loss of coordination and — the worst-case scenario — eventual collapse. If you’d like peanut butter to be one of the ingredients on your homemade dog treat repertoire, read the label carefully, as several peanut butters on the market contain xylitol.
  • Other toxic ingredients, some of which may surprise you, include chocolate and raisins. Likewise, the ever-popular jerky treats, especially those imported from China, have sickened multiple pets and even been fatal.

    When in doubt, consult the ASPCA’s Animal Poison Control Center to access its database of ingredients identified as toxic to animals. In case of a potential emergency, call 888-426-4435 if you think your pet may have eaten a poisonous substance. Plants of the genus allium, which includes onions, chives, garlic and leeks, make some pets sick (there have even been fatalities), while others don't seem affected.

    Symptoms of allium poisoning can occur a day or several days after ingestion, depending on the amount eaten. Dogs can healthfully consume 1/4 teaspoon of freshly chopped garlic per 15 pounds of body weight and reap substantial health benefits, but don't go overboard.
  • Cute shapes such as dog bones, fish, stars and paw prints are fun to make and give to your dog, but be aware that baking molds, as well as the containers you may store the treats in, may contain bisphenol A (BPA), as well as BPS (bisphenol S), a contaminant linked to cancer, hormone and cellular disruption, and other serious health problems.
  • Last but not least, the kitchen can be dangerous for dogs, particularly in terms of hot stoves and open ovens. One way to keep your pup safe while you bake is to secure your baking operation by implementing a dog gate.

If Your Dog Is on a Special Diet

It’s not a good idea to keep your dog’s dish filled to allow them access to all the food they want, whenever they want it, and the same thing goes for treats. Knowing the amount that’s optimal for your dog depends not just on their breed and age, but the amount they’re given, and that includes treats.

Treats shouldn’t comprise more than 10% of the calorie intake your dog consumes on a daily basis, although a small amount of fluctuation is acceptable at times. The remaining 90% should come from a complete and balanced, fresh species-appropriate diet.

Dr. Donna Raditic, co-founder of CANWI and board-certified veterinary nutritionist with Nutrition and Integrative Medicine Consultants in Athens, Georgia, says the best method for monitoring the amounts your dog eats is by using a scale that tells you gram weight. She explains:

“If your dog eats 100 grams a day of a food that provides 35 calories per gram, they are getting 350 calories a day. So your treats may contain 4.0 calories per gram, and if it weighs 10 grams, you are adding 40 calories. So now the total calorie intake is 390 calories, and that can really impact weight management.”3

Additionally, dogs can suffer from gum (periodontal) disease just like people, and it’s not something to ignore, especially as your dog ages. Raw bones are one type of treat that help remove tartar and plaque as they’re being chewed, which will help ensure your dog retains strong, healthy teeth.

Other Considerations When Giving (or Making) Dog Treats

Humans may be aware that what they eat themselves will constitute part of a healthy diet — one that supplies a healthy amount of vitamins and minerals, satisfies hunger, staves off disease and also tastes good. Unfortunately, you can’t always trust labels that assure dog treats are “all natural.” So what’s the best way to give your canine companion a little something extra, but ensure it’s something that will be nutritious as well as enjoyable? Needless to say, sugar- and frosting-coated treats are completely unnecessary, unhealthy and probably not even something dogs enjoy that much. Also, Jeffrey asserts, avoiding fat is important because some dogs can develop pancreatitis with high-fat treats and foods, especially if it’s hydrogenated or “interesterified.” Pancreatitis is a painful inflammation of the pancreas that can result in hospitalization for a pet.

item.title: You Probably Already Have This Pet Treat at Home
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Carrots contain beta-carotene, which may help improve your pet's health in several ways, such as boosting immune response
  • Carrots contain polyacetylenes, an organic class of compounds that have potent antimicrobial and antimycobacterial benefits, playing a key role in mycotoxin detoxification
  • You can steam and puree carrots before feeding them to your pet. If you intend to serve carrots raw, be sure to wash, peel and then cut them into bite-sized chunks
  • If your dog has a sensitive stomach, steaming carrots before feeding is recommended
  • Remember to rotate carrots with other healthy treats to make sure your pet gets a variety of nutrients to help optimize their health

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 21, 2019.

Carrots are enjoyed around the world for their flavor and crunchiness, and their inherent nutrients may benefit your health as well. Wouldn't it be great if your pet could enjoy them, too?

If the thought of feeding carrots to your pet doesn't appeal to you, it's time to reconsider. Steamed or raw, carrots can be enjoyed as a delicious snack, and they're much healthier than commercially made pet treats. In addition to being a snack, carrots can be part of a nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet. Whichever way you choose to include carrots, it'll be a win for your pet, as long as the serving size is controlled.

Where Did Carrots Come From?

Carrots were a part of prehistoric human civilization. Historians believe that the vegetable originated in Eurasia and was subsequently cultivated in China around the 11th century before reaching Europe during the 13th century.1 Today, China, Uzbekistan and Russia are the top carrot producers of the world.2

The Principal Phytonutrient of Carrots — Beta-Carotene

Perhaps the greatest claim to fame of carrots is their beta-carotene content, a precursor phytonutrient (as well as a carotenoid) that transforms into vitamin A in dogs (cats need to consume preformed vitamin A directly from meat sources3). Beta-carotene is also responsible for the common orange color of carrots.4

Beta-carotene may be one of the most important nutrients for boosting your dog's immune health. In one noteworthy study, researchers had this encouraging conclusion about beta-carotene for dogs:5

"In summary, older dogs have lower immunological responses compared with younger controls. Beta-carotene supplementation significantly restored immune responses in older dogs when compared with their age-matched controls and younger counterparts."

As dogs age, they may develop poor eyesight, just like humans. However, beta-carotene, along with other carotenoids, may help reverse that problem. A study published in the Journal of Nutritional Science found that dogs that received carotenoids had improvements in various eyesight functions.6

Did You Know?

In the off chance you have a rabbit, don't give them carrots on a regular basis. Bugs Bunny was wrong all along!

Daily carrots fed to rabbits can harm their health because of too much carbohydrates.7 The carrot-eating habit of Bugs Bunny was actually inspired by Clark Gable's portrayal of Peter Warne in the movie "It Happened One Night."8

Other Phytochemicals in Carrots

Carrots also contain other phytochemicals, namely phenolics, polyacetylenes and ascorbic acid. According to a 2019 study, these substances can bring various benefits to the table:9

"These chemicals aid in the risk reduction of cancer and cardiovascular diseases due to their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, plasma lipid modification, and anti-tumor properties."

Ascorbic acid, commonly known as vitamin C, is an essential nutrient that should be obtained from the environment regularly, and its importance is well-documented. According to the Canadian Journal of Veterinary Research, vitamin C is a crucial cofactor "for enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of collagen, carnitine and norepinephrine." Furthermore, vitamin C has antioxidant capabilities.10

Meanwhile, in vitro studies of polyacetylenes show their potential against cancer. They're toxic to various cancer cell lines as well as possess potent "antifungal, anti-inflammatory and anti-platelet aggregatory characteristics."11 As for phenolics, they act as an antioxidant protecting against reactive oxygen species.12

Polyacetylenes also play a key role in detoxifying the body from mycotoxins13 (including aflatoxin B1). Mycotoxin contamination is one of the main reasons for pet food recalls,14,15 and research shows many brands of pet food contain mycotoxins that can damage your pet's organs and create disease.16,17

Fun Fact About Carrots

The "carot" in "beta-carotene" was derived, literally, from carrots by German chemist Heinrich Wilhelm Ferdinand Wackenroder back in 1831. During one of his experiments, he extracted beta-carotene by pressing out the juice of carrots, then isolated it with ether.18

Preparing Carrot Treats for Your Pet

Misinformation about many healthy fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds abounds on the internet. This is because websites have labeled all risks (such as the risk of over-consumption causing gastrointestinal issues, or choking on too large of pieces or pits) as "toxicities," which isn't true, but has managed to confuse millions of pet lovers, nonetheless.

That being said, carrots have none of those problems, as long as you offer them in very small pieces to avoid choking risks and you feed them to your pet in moderate quantities.

"You should also choose certified organic produce, whenever possible. Make sure to purchase organic or 'spray-free' carrots from certified producers."

According to the Environmental Working Group (EWG), carrots rank 13th in their "2026 Shopper's Guide to Pesticides in Produce™."19 This means that the carrots found in your grocery store are likely to be sprayed with pesticides, but they're not among the most heavily contaminated "Dirty Dozen."

Raw carrots should be cut into bite-sized pieces so they're easy to chew. Wash the carrots thoroughly and peel them, especially if they aren't organic.20 Here are other suggestions when feeding carrots to your pets:21

  • Grate a carrot to use as a topping for their meals.
  • After cooking a carrot, mash and mix a little bit into their dinner.
  • Slice carrots into chips and dehydrate them. Dried carrot slices are excellent, shelf-stable treats.
  • If your dog has a sensitive stomach, steaming carrots before feeding is recommended.22
  • With supervision, large, frozen carrots may be beneficial for teething puppies and can be a cheaper alternative to chew toys. These may help ease their teething pain and enhance dental health.23

Again, when feeding treats to your pet, limit the amount to less than 10% of your pet's daily caloric intake. The bulk of your pet's nutrition should still come from a species-appropriate diet. Treats are only there to serve as a healthy snack — they should not be considered as a replacement meal.

Go Ahead and Give the Occasional Carrots to Your Pet

The verdict is in — carrots can be a nutritious, occasional treat for your pet, provided they come from certified organic sources and are given in the recommended amounts. Remember to rotate carrots with other healthy treats to make sure your pet gets a variety of nutrients to help optimize their health.

item.title: Dogs Mimic Their Owners' Facial Expressions
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Dogs were found to display rapid mimicry of the other dogs’ body movements, particularly a play bow, and facial expression (a relaxed, open mouth)
  • Dogs were more likely to mimic familiar, socially bonded companions. Rapid mimicry occurred in 77% of dogs, extended play sessions, and may reflect empathy-like emotional contagion that strengthens relationships
  • Within less than one second of seeing another dog play bow or relax their facial expression, many of the dogs responded in suit, copying the other dog’s expression or behavior
  • The dogs’ level of familiarity with one another affected their level of mimicry; dogs that already knew each other and were socially bonded were more likely to mimic each other
  • Dogs can likely mimic their owners’ facial expressions as well, especially if they’re closely bonded

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 26, 2017.

Are dogs empathetic beings, capable of experiencing others' emotions? Very likely, yes, according to research published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.1 The study involved dozens of dogs, which were observed at a dog park in Italy.

Many of the dogs were found to display rapid mimicry of the other dogs' body movements, particularly a play bow and facial expression (a relaxed, open mouth).

Within less than one second of seeing another dog play bow or relax their facial expression, many of the dogs responded in suit, copying the other dog's expression or behavior.

What's more, the dogs' level of familiarity with one another affected their level of mimicry. Dogs that already knew each other and were socially bonded were more likely to mimic each other. "The stronger the social bonding, the higher the level of rapid mimicry," the researchers wrote.2

The findings are incredibly intriguing, because facial mimicry in humans and non-human primates is a form of emotional contagion that is regarded as a basic form of empathy.

Overall, a high level of rapid mimicry was observed in a mean of 77% of the dogs, which reacted after perceiving play bows or a relaxed, open mouth facial expression.3

When the dogs mimicked each other, their play sessions lasted longer, which suggests it increased the dogs' motivation to play and possibly strengthened the dogs' relationship.

Dogs May Mimic Owners' Facial Expressions, Too

If you smile at your dog, does he smile back? The researchers believe, given their findings that dogs mimic the emotional states of other dogs, that dogs can mimic their owners' facial expressions as well, especially if they're closely bonded. Seeker reported:4

"'It is an automatic response, similar to that of humans when they see someone crying or smiling,' [lead author Elisabetta] Palagi [,Ph.D.,] said, adding that domestication probably even enhanced dogs' natural inclination toward emotional contagion all the more."

The totality of evidence is showing that dogs have many complex ways of communicating with and understanding not only other dogs but also humans.

The researchers pointed out that dogs follow others' gaze, head and body orientation, and combine body postures, including head and tail movements, to communicate their emotional states.

They also use their eyes, lips and teeth expressively and "regularly express their positive emotional states via specific signals that are performed through both the face (relaxed open mouth … and the body (play bow)."

Further, dogs can discriminate between emotional expressions on human faces and body postures. For instance, research published in Biology Letters found dogs recognize both dog and human emotions.5

The dogs were presented with either human or dog faces with different expressions (happy and playful versus angry and aggressive). The faces were paired with a vocalization that was positive, negative or neutral.

The dogs looked significantly longer at the faces that matched up to the appropriate vocalization, which is an ability previously thought to be distinct to humans.

STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • D-mannose is a naturally occurring simple sugar found in cranberries and other fruits that helps prevent E. coli — the cause of about 30% to 60% of pet urinary tract infections (UTIs) depending on the study — from sticking to the bladder wall, so bacteria get flushed out during normal urination instead of colonizing the urinary tract

  • The strongest evidence comes from human studies in women with recurrent UTIs, where D-mannose reduced recurrence rates dramatically (down to about 15% versus 60% with no prophylaxis) and produced far fewer side effects than preventive antibiotics
  • Veterinary research is more limited but supportive, and a 2022 AHVMA review recommends D-mannose as a standard preventive measure for pets with recurrent UTIs
  • D-mannose is best suited for preventing recurrence in pets with a history of E. coli UTIs, not as a first-line treatment for an active infection — bladder stones, tumors, non-E. coli bacteria, and biofilm-protected infections all require separate veterinary evaluation and treatment

Your dog has been squatting to pee every few minutes and coming up with a dribble. Your cat is making frequent, unproductive trips to the litter box, and you notice a spot of blood. You have been through this before. The veterinary clinic, the culture, the antibiotics, and the wait for the next flare-up.

Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) are exhausting for pets and pet parents alike. And while antibiotics still have their essential role, a growing number of veterinarians are also reaching for a much quieter tool. It is a naturally occurring sugar called D-mannose, and its job is simple: make life a lot harder for the bacteria trying to take up residence in your pet's bladder.

Why UTIs Are So Common in Pets

UTIs are one of the most frequent reasons dogs and cats end up at the veterinary clinic. Estimates suggest that 14%1 to 27% of dogs will have at least one UTI in their lifetime, with females at higher risk due to their shorter urethra. Cats are less commonly affected overall with bacterial urinary tract infection, but lower-tract urinary problems are still the No. 1 reason cats end up in the clinic.2,3,4

A frequent culprit is E. coli, which is responsible for about 80% of community-acquired UTIs in people and about 30% to 60% in pets.5,6 Common triggers include incomplete bladder emptying, bladder stones, diabetes, obesity, post-surgical catheter use, immunosuppressive drugs, and simply not drinking enough water.7,8

Some pets get one UTI and never have another. Others develop chronic patterns where infections keep returning despite antibiotics. It is that second group where D-mannose really shines.9,10

What D-Mannose Actually Is

D-mannose is a simple, naturally occurring six-carbon sugar. It is found in small amounts in fruits like cranberries, apples, oranges, peaches, blueberries, and mangoes. It is closely related to glucose but behaves very differently once it is in the body.

The most important difference is that D-mannose is not really metabolized. In humans, about 90% of ingested D-mannose is absorbed and then quickly filtered out of the bloodstream by the kidneys, ending up in the urine largely unchanged. That is exactly where you want it.11,12

Because it is not metabolized like other sugars, it does not raise blood sugar or affect urinary pH in meaningful ways. That also makes it a reasonable option for pets with diabetes, though always with veterinary guidance.13,14

The Sweet Trick

Here is the elegant part. Most UTI-causing E. coli (and certain other types of bacteria) use tiny hair-like projections called fimbriae to grab onto the cells lining the bladder wall. Those fimbriae carry a specialized receptor (called FimH15) that looks for mannose-like sugars.

When there is enough D-mannose in the urine, the bacteria latch onto it instead of the bladder lining. Once they are bound to a sugar molecule floating in the urine, they can no longer stick to the bladder lining. They get flushed out during normal urination. Think of it like coating the inside of the bladder with something so slick that bacteria cannot get a grip — like “molecular Teflon.”16,17

Why This Approach Is Different

Antibiotics kill bacteria. Because of this, bacteria are under evolutionary pressure to survive by developing resistance. Every course of antibiotics used contributes to that pressure, which is why antibiotic resistance has become such a significant issue in both human and veterinary medicine.

D-mannose does not kill anything. It does not damage bacteria, disrupt their function, or interfere with their metabolism. It just makes them slippery. That means there is no meaningful path for bacteria to become resistant to it.

It also plays nicely with antibiotics. There are no known negative interactions between D-mannose and antibiotic therapy, and some veterinarians pair the two in stubborn cases for a multi-pronged approach.18,19

D-Mannose vs. Cranberry

Cranberry has a long history as a UTI supplement. And D-mannose is actually one of the compounds in cranberry that gives it its benefit. But cranberry contains other useful compounds too, most notably proanthocyanidins, which are antioxidants that may work through a slightly different mechanism to keep bacteria from adhering.20

Purified D-mannose is often preferred in pets for a few reasons. It is more concentrated, cranberry juice tends to be too sugary for pets, and D-mannose is generally considered better for quick action on an existing bacterial issue. Cranberry powder or extract is more often positioned for longer-term urinary support.21

Some veterinarians and integrative practitioners combine the two, since their mechanisms are different enough that they may work in synergy. Human studies have shown higher cure and remission rates when cranberry and D-mannose are used together alongside antibiotics.22

What the Research Actually Shows

Most of the strong human research on D-mannose has been in women with recurrent UTIs, and the results have been generally favorable. Multiple studies have shown that D-mannose reduces the rate of recurrence, extends the time between infections, and produces significantly fewer side effects than preventive antibiotics.

In one randomized trial in women, D-mannose reduced the recurrence rate to 14.6% compared to 60.8% in women receiving no prophylaxis, a result on par with the antibiotic nitrofurantoin.23,24

Dedicated placebo-controlled studies in dogs and cats are more limited, and much of the veterinary evidence comes from case series, reviews, and clinical experience. A 2022 AHVMA scientific review concluded that D-mannose should be considered a standard preventive measure when planning care for pets with recurrent UTIs, citing its low cost, low side-effect profile, and lack of resistance risk.25

You need to remember, though, that D-mannose is not a first-line treatment for an active UTI in dogs. However, it may be recommended as part of a broader plan to reduce risk in dogs prone to recurrent infections.26

Where It Fits Best

D-mannose is not a cure-all. It works well in specific situations and less well in others. Here is where it tends to shine and where it falls short.27,28,29

Where D-mannose is a strong fit:

  • Preventing recurrence in pets with a history of E. coli UTIs
  • Adding to antibiotic therapy for stubborn or repeat infections
  • Long-term daily support for pets at increased UTI risk
  • Pets with diabetes, since it is largely non-metabolized
  • Situations where reducing antibiotic exposure is a priority

Where D-mannose is not the right answer:

  • Active, complicated UTIs, which still need veterinary diagnosis and antibiotics
  • UTIs caused by bacteria that do not have mannose receptors (some strains of E. coli, and many other species, are unaffected)
  • Infections protected by bacterial biofilms, which can shield bacteria from both antibiotics and mannose
  • Bladder stones, crystals, or urinary tumors, which are separate problems requiring their own workup

If D-mannose is going to help, most owners report seeing symptom improvement within 48 to 72 hours. If nothing has changed after about three days, that is your cue to head back to the vet.

Dosing and Administration

Standardized canine dosing has not been formally established, but veterinary sources have converged on a general range. Common suggestions include:30,31

  • Small dogs (up to 15 pounds) — 250 to 500 milligrams (mg)
  • Medium dogs (16 to 50 lb.) — 500 mg to 1 gram (g)
  • Large dogs (51 to 95 lb.) — 1 to 1.5 g
  • Giant dogs (96 lb and up) — 1.5 to 2 g
  • Cats — About 250 to 500 mg once daily, twice daily if symptoms persist

Because D-mannose clears the bloodstream and lands in the urine quickly, splitting the daily dose into two or three servings helps keep steady levels in the bladder. Start on the lower end for prevention, and lean higher for a flare-up under veterinary guidance.32

The powder is inexpensive, tastes mildly sweet, and mixes easily into moistened food. Dog-specific formulations may include probiotics, cranberry, or other urinary support ingredients. Skip human-formulated supplements without checking with your veterinarian, since they may include ingredients that are not dog-safe.33,34

Safety and Side Effects

D-mannose is generally very well tolerated in dogs and cats. When side effects do occur, they are usually mild digestive changes such as loose stool or gas. If you notice any GI symptoms after starting D-mannose, stop the product and check in with your veterinarian. A few cautions worth knowing:35,36

  • Talk to your vet before starting D-mannose in pets with kidney insufficiency, since reduced clearance may change how it behaves in the body
  • Pregnant and lactating pets should only receive it under veterinary direction
  • Diabetic pets can usually take it safely because it does not raise blood sugar meaningfully, but confirm with your veterinarian before starting
  • Use a dog- or cat-specific product rather than a human supplement, and follow your vet's dosing instructions exactly

Beyond the Supplement: A Fuller Prevention Plan

Even the best supplement is only part of the picture. A well-rounded UTI-prevention plan for pets usually includes the following, and making adjustments here can dramatically lower the odds of a recurrence:

  • Plenty of water — offer multiple bowls, consider a pet fountain, add water or broth to meals
  • Wet or canned food for pets who need extra hydration, especially cats
  • Frequent potty breaks so dogs are not holding urine for long stretches; ideally, a dog should have access to empty their bladder at least every 4 hours
  • A clean, accessible litter box for cats — many cats will hold it if the box is dirty
  • Keeping the rear-end area clean, trimming long hair around the vulva or prepuce
  • Weight management — obesity has been associated with higher UTI risk
  • A veterinarian-recommended diet if your pet is prone to struvite crystals or stones
  • Routine urinalysis at annual or bi-annual checkups to catch trouble early

When to Call the Vet

D-mannose is a preventive and supportive tool, not a substitute for veterinary care. Some situations always call for immediate professional attention:

  • Straining to urinate or producing only tiny amounts
  • Blood in the urine
  • A cat unable to pass urine at all — this can be a life-threatening emergency, especially in males
  • Fever, vomiting, sudden lethargy, or abdominal pain
  • No urine produced for 12 hours
  • Symptoms lasting more than about three days despite D-mannose; remember, urinary tract infections are painful and we do not want our pets to be in pain

Blocked urethras are extremely painful and can be fatal within hours. When in doubt, treat urinary distress as an emergency.37

Small Sugar, Big Difference

There is something appealingly simple about a therapy that does not fight bacteria at all — it just makes them slide right out of the body. D-mannose works because of a small quirk of chemistry: the same receptors that let E. coli grip the bladder wall also happen to be a perfect fit for a sweet, safe sugar.

It is not a miracle. It does not replace a good veterinarian, a clean sample, a proper culture, or the right antibiotic when one is needed. But for pets who keep circling back to the clinic with the same infection, D-mannose is a well-tolerated, science-backed way to tip the odds back in their favor — and sometimes to skip the next round of antibiotics entirely.

If your pet has been dealing with recurring urinary trouble, talk with your veterinarian about whether D-mannose belongs in the plan. Sometimes the simplest tools turn out to be the ones that finally break the cycle.

  • Symptoms lasting more than about three days despite D-mannose; remember, urinary tract infections are painful and we do not want our pets to be in pain

Blocked urethras are extremely painful and can be fatal within hours. When in doubt, treat urinary distress as an emergency.37

Small Sugar, Big Difference

There is something appealingly simple about a therapy that does not fight bacteria at all — it just makes them slide right out of the body. D-mannose works because of a small quirk of chemistry: the same receptors that let E. coli grip the bladder wall also happen to be a perfect fit for a sweet, safe sugar.

It is not a miracle. It does not replace a good veterinarian, a clean sample, a proper culture, or the right antibiotic when one is needed. But for pets who keep circling back to the clinic with the same infection, D-mannose is a well-tolerated, science-backed way to tip the odds back in their favor — and sometimes to skip the next round of antibiotics entirely.

If your pet has been dealing with recurring urinary trouble, talk with your veterinarian about whether D-mannose belongs in the plan. Sometimes the simplest tools turn out to be the ones that finally break the cycle.
